name: Base Pair to kDa Calculator
seoTitle: Base Pair to kDa Calculator — Formula & Results
seoDesc: Kilodaltons and base pairs convert with one factor: 0.65 kDa per base pair of double-stranded DNA. Free base pair to kda calculator: enter your values and get
summary:
Kilodaltons and base pairs convert with one factor: 0.65 kDa per base pair of double-stranded DNA. It returns DNA mass, encoded amino acids, protein mass and DNA per kDa of protein, and the panel shows all of them at once.

This calculator does both. The arithmetic keeps full precision internally and only rounds what it displays, so the number you copy out is the number the formula produced. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the Base Pair to kDa
sections.html:
DNA: kDa = bp × 0.65; protein: kDa ≈ (bp ÷ 3) × 0.11

The symbols in the formula
SymbolWhat it stands forUnit
bplength in base pairsbp
0.65kDa per base pair of dsDNAkDa/bp
0.11average kDa per amino acidkDa/aa

sections.title: How do I use the Base Pair to kDa?
sections.html:
Fill the boxes you have numbers for; the calculator decides what it can derive from them.

  1. Enter the values you already have. Every box accepts a decimal point and a minus sign; thousands separators are ignored.
  2. The grey boxes are results: they are worked out from your inputs and cannot be typed into.
  3. Press Calculate. The results fill in together, and from then on they follow every edit you make — there is no page to reload and nothing to submit.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html:
Take the default values the page opens with: dna length of 3,000 bp.

Substituting them into the formula gives dna mass of 1,950 kDa, encoded amino acids of 1,000, protein mass of 110 kDa, dna per kda of protein of 27.27 bp.

Because the example uses the defaults, you can reproduce it by loading the page and reading the results panel before touching anything.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• The protein estimate assumes the whole sequence is one open reading frame with no introns — true for bacterial genes and cDNA, wrong for genomic eukaryotic sequence.

  • Average residue mass is about 110 Da; a protein rich in glycine (57 Da) or tryptophan (186 Da) will deviate, and the estimate is only good to about ±10%.

  • For a fusion protein, add the tag: 6×His is about 0.8 kDa and GST about 26 kDa.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
Before blaming the formula, check these — they explain nearly every mismatch:

  • Converting a eukaryotic gene length straight to protein mass, introns included.
  • Forgetting the stop codon, which does not become an amino acid.
  • Using 0.65 kDa per bp for single-stranded RNA, where it is about 0.34.

How big is the protein from a 1 500 bp open reading frame?
What does the Base Pair to kDa actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns DNA mass, encoded amino acids, protein mass and DNA per kDa of protein. Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. This calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.

faq.q: Can I use it with the numbers straight from a datasheet?
faq.a: Yes. Every box states its unit, and nothing is converted behind your back, so a figure copied from a datasheet, a kit insert or a protocol goes in as printed.
